posts.text:
At what point does “economic development” become a revolving door?

Follow the names, then ask why so many roads lead back to Greg Abbott.

Texas recruits the companies and Corporate executives get seats inside the state’s economic-development apparatus. Government officials leave office and later represent technology vendors doing business in the same Texas market.

Then the same names start showing up together on India-facing business organizations and official Texas trade missions.

This didn’t happen for JUST one appointment - It’s a pattern.

Sanjiv Yajnik → TxEDC presiding officer.

Wipro CEO Abid Neemuchwala → Abbott-appointed TxEDC director.

Arun Agarwal → TxEDC vice chair → Abbott India delegation → TxEDC chairman.

Robert Allen → Abbott deputy chief of staff → TxEDC CEO.

And of course - going the other direction:

David Whitley → Abbott deputy chief / Secretary of State → later represents Wipro, Accenture and Nextt.

John B. Scott → Abbott-appointed DIR presiding officer / Secretary of State → later represents Deloitte.

Jerry Strickland → longtime Abbott adviser → later represents Cognizant.

Then the circle gets smaller:

Yajnik. Agarwal. Neemuchwala. Manish Vyas of Tech Mahindra.

They appear together again inside the Indian American CEO Council.

I’m not claiming these relationships prove bribery, contract steering or a quid pro quo.

I’m asking something simpler:

HOW MANY TIMES CAN THE SAME PEOPLE MOVE BETWEEN GOVERNMENT, ECONOMIC-DEVELOPMENT BOARDS, INDIA MISSIONS, TECHNOLOGY COMPANIES AND LOBBYING BEFORE TEXANS DESERVE TO SEE THE WHOLE NETWORK?

Texas doesn’t show it this way.

The appointments are over here, Lobbying records over there and Contracts somewhere else. Trade missions get press releases, Board memberships get biographies and if you aren’t looking - you’ll miss it.

Individually, each record looks ordinary, but when put together, the revolving door becomes visible.

Texans shouldn’t need an investigation to learn who has been moving between public power and private interests. 

So I put the records together.

And @GregAbbott_TX has some explaining to do.

posts.text:
如果共和党输掉了德州的中期选举？

这个提问，放在六个月之前，那是大逆不道。

哪怕放在昨天之前，也有点痴人说梦。

但昨天，在共和党老巢的核心，德州达拉斯，共和党中期选举全国动员大会，在川普上场时，竟然也只上坐了6到7成。

美国航空中心会场容量大约2万到2.1万人。官方事先说票卖完了，要来2万多人，川普也反复讲座无虚席、外面还有人进不去。但多家媒体报道的实际是：
靠近舞台的地板区和下层坐得比较满，中上层、上层看台大片空着。有记者估计川普上台时大约六到七成满。开场时更空，工作人员临近开场还在发免费票。

这是达拉斯，还是总统、副总统和共和党领袖人物都到场，还是全党举全国之力第一次搞这种“期中大会”。这样的上座率已经充分说明了问题。

这次联邦中期选举，德州有一个参议员位置要竞选，Paxton（共和党） vs. Talarico（民主党） 已经被认为是全国关键战场之一。多个民调显示，民主党候选人已经稍微领先，而昨天的达拉斯，还是共和党候选人Paxton的长期根据地。

德州州长也是这次中期选举的重头戏。目前现任州长Abbott仍然略占优势，但民主党候选人Hinojosa已经把竞争拉到了非常接近的程度；路透社甚至把2026德州州长选举描述为民主党真正有机会突破的战场。

让我们看看历史：德州已经有30多年沒有出出现过民主党联邦参议员。德州现任共和党州长已经稳稳连任了三届，这次寻求第四任。

如果在德州共和党这次参议员竞选输了，代表德州开始翻蓝，如果连州长都输了，那就是“红州变蓝”的历史转折。

还记得加州吗？共和党失去后，几十年都拿不回来。

加州，德州，是全美经济最发达的两个州，也是人口最多的两个州。

如果这次输掉了德州，意味着共和党的天都塌了。

德州，对于共和党，其重要性怎么阐述都不为过。

以至于德州共和党参议员候选人Paxton自己在达拉斯大会上说的很直白：“如果我们失去了德克萨斯州，我们就失去了常识革命。如果我们失去了常识革命，我们就失去了美国。” 

德州会不会开始翻蓝？共和党是否能赢得历史上最重要的一次中期选举？川普是选举助力还是票房毒药？

所有的谜底，将在11月3号揭开。

posts.name: S.E. Robinson, Jr.
posts.text:
TESLA: Yesterday evening Lamar CISD trustees voted unanimously in Rosenberg to advance the JETI application for the $10.1B proposed Project Crystal in Fort Bend County. 

David Denison of Kroll, Tesla’s JETI advisor, said the 2029–2038 M&O tax limitation would narrow a cost gap. Tesla projects 9,712 permanent jobs by 2033 and $1.3 billion annual payroll.

Board President Jacci Hotzel backed the vote after a public hearing. The Texas Comptroller had recommended approval August 31st.

The filing now goes to Gov. Greg Abbott. If, and when, Abbott agrees, Tesla, Lamar CISD, and the governor move to a three-party JETI agreement. 

Technically Tesla has not chosen the Fort Bend site yet. It is still comparing that location with one outside Texas. Site selection, land deals, local permits, and any other tax abatements sit outside the JETI vote. So we shall see. 

Construction in the application is listed for 2026–2028, with commercial operations targeted for Q1 2029.

Update on this: Christian Castro was finally arrested in Minneapolis on Wednesday. It took Abbott's stall tactic running out the clock, not any change of heart. A federal judge denied Minnesota's extradition request outright, Castro sat out a 90-day detention window in a Texas jail, and Abbott let him walk free on August 27th rather than hand him over. 

He was only re-arrested after a federal grand jury indicted him in early September, on charges of lying to investigators, the first DOJ prosecution of a federal officer for misconduct anywhere in Operation Metro Surge.

His attorney says Castro always meant to face the charges and drove voluntarily to Minneapolis to surrender. Maybe so. But eight months in his home state while a Republican governor blocked the one mechanism that could have brought him back isn't "wanting his day in court." It's what accountability looks like when it's finally forced through.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said it best: "Governor Abbott's attempt to shield Mr. Castro from accountability has failed. We look forward to commencing our prosecution." 

Castro is due in Minneapolis state court today, and in federal court in St. Paul tomorrow morning.

posts.text:
Hey Texas, if a data center or a giant transmission line is showing up near you, this is the conversation that you will want to be certain you participate in.

This morning the Public Utility Commission of Texas posted an update in Project 58317. PUCT is a state agency. It regulates electric utilities across Texas. ERCOT is one of the grids in this state, but not the only one. If you live here, this file is about your bill, your water, your land, and what gets built next door to your home.

Here’s the short version of what’s going on.

PUCT just filed a new roadmap for the large-load rules coming out of Senate Bill 6. Some of those rules are already adopted. They’re now drafting a standard interconnection agreement; basically the contract data centers will sign to hook up and the terms for who pays. At the same time, Governor Abbott’s audit is still running. The first official write-up is being aimed at December. That’s the date to beat.

The Governor has also told other agencies to lock arms on this:

Data centers are supposed to pay for their own electric infrastructure, not pass it to households.

Projects in the queue are supposed to be checked: power, water, ownership, tax breaks, impact on neighbors.

On Sept. 14 he told the Texas Water Development Board to enforce water-use reporting and work the water side of the audit.

Yesterday he told TCEQ to stop issuing data-center permits until those audits are done.

Those letters are already in this docket. Your comment can sit right next to them if you follow the steps listed in this post.

Here’s the part that should bother you. As of today there are 69 filings in 58317. Since the August audit started, only about 40 to 45 public comments have actually been filed. Meanwhile a lot more people are saying they oppose these projects at town halls, in group chats, and in the comments. Talking about it online feels like doing something. It isn’t the official record. If it isn’t filed, the agency can move on like you never spoke.

This is how regular people talk to their government. Not a petition that disappears. Not a rant that only your friends see. A short letter in the docket that staff and commissioners have to keep.

It takes a few minutes:

Write what you know. Your name, your city or county, the project near you, and what you’ve seen; higher bills, water worries, a substation, a 765 kV route, trucks, noise, whatever is real for you. Save it as a PDF. Don’t put account numbers or other private details in it. These filings are public.

Go to https://t.co/dcoWcbjVDk
Hit Begin, check the box, and type Control Number 58317

Put in your contact info. Filing Party is just your name.
Filing Type: Comments
Description can be simple: Public comments on data centers, 765 kV, and the Governor’s audit
Upload the PDF and submit. Keep the confirmation email.

You can read everything already filed by searching 58317 on the Interchange.

If you live in Texas and this is in your backyard, or you just don’t want households paying for someone else’s megawatts: FILE IT . Then send this to one neighbor who has been loud online and quiet on paper. December is when the first audit packet comes together. Get your name in the file before that.

Do you really want your government to be able to say they gave you a chance to participate and only 40 people did? Or to say that the internet was all bots that were concerned and not real people because real people did not show up to the conversation? Have you submitted your concerns to the Docket? If not... what are you waiting for?

December, that is your deadline. ⏰️

posts.name: ErinEpley
posts.text:
This is a fact-driven account of why Ken Paxton was impeached—and why those facts matter now that he is asking Texans to send him to the United States Senate. I am grateful that The Dallas Morning News gave space to this evidence and to why it still matters. 

You can read the published version here: https://t.co/JfJkbXVncP.

Because the published version is available only to subscribers, below is the essay as I submitted it.
—-
Impeachment prosecutor: Ken Paxton is unfit for office

The evidence against him is relevant again now that he’s asking for our votes.
 
Three years ago this month, Attorney General Ken Paxton faced removal from office by the Texas Senate after being impeached by the Texas House, 121 to 23. The vote was remarkable. Sixty Republicans joined 61 Democrats. More than 70% of House Republicans voted to impeach a member of their own party. This once straight-ticket Republican voter was proud.
 
I served as chief counsel to the Texas House General Investigating Committee, led the investigation into Paxton, and later served as a trial attorney in the Senate. Those facts matter now because Paxton is asking Texans to send him to the United States Senate.
 
The central story behind Paxton’s impeachment is less complicated than volumes of evidence make it seem: Paxton relentlessly used the Office of the Attorney General for the private benefit of his friend and donor, Nate Paul, and received benefits from Paul in the form of home renovations.
 
Here’s how: Paxton pressed his office to release its copy of the federal criminal investigation of Paul to Paul — an extraordinary break from policy. He advocated against a Texas bank and charity. He directed his staff to enter litigation in which the state was not needed and demanded that the charity accept millions less than it was entitled to receive from Paul. Another unnecessary intervention prevented a Texas bank from foreclosing on a multimillion-dollar asset tied to Paul.
 
Paxton also attempted to use government power to intrude into Texans’ private records. He installed a secret “prosecutor” as Paul’s personal resource, answerable only to Paxton, Paul and Paul’s attorney. The man was given a title he did not know was fake and an agreement he did not know was invalid. He was never paid or entered into the OAG human resources system. Paxton instructed him to take direction from Paul’s attorney and use OAG resources against Paul’s perceived enemies.
 
Thirty-nine subpoenas targeting Texas citizens followed. The arrangement remained hidden until an alert banker called the OAG.
 
Each action served to aid Paul’s federal criminal defense or save him millions owed to others.
 
All of this was presented as evidence during Paxton’s trial. He used the weight of his office and powers hidden from public view to enrich himself and his friend. In my opinion, that is abuse of office. It is disqualifying.
 
Then there were the renovations to Paxton’s home. Paul is a real estate developer. By Paxton’s own account, upgrades related to Paul were worth at least $121,000. We know because that is what Paxton ultimately paid, after he was caught getting them for free.
 
Records and testimony link the upgrades directly to Paul. The work was completed by July 2020, yet there were no charges.
 
On Sept. 30, 2020, Paxton’s senior staff reported him to the FBI for bribery and abuse of office related to the subpoenas and renovations linked to Paul. Paxton then directed an unsolicited payment to the purported contractor.
 
There were no estimates, invoices or payments before Sept. 30. Metadata shows the lone invoice was created Oct. 1. It was backdated to appear to have been issued on Sept. 1. It was not delivered.
 
For me, the facts preceding Sept. 30 sufficiently establish bribery and abuse of office. The Sept. 30 payment after the report solidifies it. The Oct. 1 backdated invoice is simply offensive.

德克萨斯州长候选人，希诺霍萨 (Gina Hinojosa) 出手要求查阅竞争对手，即现任州长格雷格·阿博特 (Greg Abbott)与埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 及其公司之间未经删减的通信记录。
此前，去年公布的约 1400 页记录已被大量删减。  州政府此前辩称，部分通信记录可以不予公开，因为其中包含“私密且令人尴尬的信息”。 希诺霍萨今天致信阿博特办公室，援引了《德克萨斯州公共信息法》中关于立法者为立法目的索取信息的条款。她要求查阅此前已向德克萨斯新闻编辑室 (Texas Newsroom) 公布的相同记录，但“不得进行任何删减”，包括被认为“令人尴尬”或“私密”的内容。 
希诺霍萨表示，这些记录可能揭示马斯克与阿博特之间的关系，包括马斯克公司获得的利润丰厚的州政府合同和税收优惠，以及马斯克的竞选捐款。她认为马斯克已将德克萨斯州变成了企业的游乐场，并表示需要提高透明度，以揭露她所说的阿博特与强大的科技利益集团之间存在的腐败关系。 她要求阿博特办公室安排在10月13日左右对已编辑和未编辑的记录进行查阅。  现在，德克萨斯州民众或许终于可以了解那些被认为“极其私密和令人尴尬”以至于被隐瞒的信息了。

posts.name: Jason Corley
posts.text:
Maybe, but let’s walk through it without suspending belief at the very beginning. First, today’s results show a Siena’s     Senate: D +6 and Governor: D +10 swing from their June from their June survey. Useful to know so we can see what needed to happen to get there. 

Texas LV sample recalls 2024 at Trump +7 in a state he won by roughly 14. Already we’re at a sizable leftward gap, but let’s allow that it’s potentially indicative of the midterm penalty/environment. To get there, however, we’re going to need a PID+lean at only R+3 according to their findings.

Then the current ballot, and therefore the likely electorate measured, moves even further left, with Talarico +6 and Hinojosa also leading Abbott +4. 

So aside from the recall/composition question. You’re also asking the electorate to produce another substantial persuasion gap on top of it. This is no small ask. Here is where we might begin suspending some belief.

None of that proves the poll is all the way wrong, but it does raise enough questions about the findings to question most of the direction and magnitude. Recall is imperfect, and I hope more people now see that, especially if they’re inclined to weight by it. I’m not absolutely opposed to the practice but I have my own studies. 

In any case, PID moves every cycle, and 2026 is a penalty environment for Republicans. But when the sample is already well left of the 2024 electorate, again, let’s allow for that, and both statewide races leap even further left still, I think it’s perfectly reasonable to scrutinize the LV model, composition, or some common-mode effect, as I said previously. 

You can of course believe all of it but you’ll have to ignore everything that got it there.

posts.text:
TEXAS DECLARES A DIESEL DISASTER, AS AMERICA EXPORTS FUEL AND FUNDS THE WAR

Truckers are under growing pressure as diesel prices rise. In less than a month, 16 trucking and transportation companies have filed for bankruptcy, five in Texas alone.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has declared a diesel disaster, easing rules on dyed diesel, truck weights, and emissions to move more fuel while Texas diesel averages about $5.86 per gallon.

The U.S. produces significant fuel, yet exports well over 1 million barrels of distillate fuel daily, including diesel. Texas is responding to a diesel emergency while American fuel continues leaving the country.

Refining is another constraint. Crude oil is not diesel; it must be processed, and U.S. refineries already run near capacity. Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the administration is pursuing the first major new U.S. refinery in decades, while President Trump says the U.S. is taking Venezuelan oil to help refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Trump has linked high oil prices to the Iran war. He also says Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries are driving the diesel problem. Iran is disrupting oil markets.

Ukraine is striking Russian refineries that produce diesel. Two wars are hitting different parts of the same energy system. If the White House believes Ukraine’s attacks are raising diesel costs for Americans, why continue managing the consequences at home instead of stopping the strikes? Washington is still supporting Ukraine, committing nearly all of its remaining $400 million in congressionally approved security aid, including offensive weapons.

That contradiction is now colliding with Texas politics. Trump is campaigning in Texas a month before the midterms, as polling shows the Senate race tightening in a state Republicans have dominated for decades.

Higher diesel costs hit truckers first. Then they raise the cost of moving everything, and eventually, the cost of nearly everything Americans buy.

Mike Adams breaks down what the diesel crisis could mean for energy supplies and the U.S. economy.

Why should Texas Republicans keep allowing Gov. Abbott to bully them into supporting government-funded, government-regulated “universal school choice”? Texas budgeted $1 billion for its Education Savings Account program, officially called Texas Education Freedom Accounts (TEFA), in the 2026–2027 state budget. The program begins with the 2026–2027 school year.

That is $1,000,000,000 in state funding for the initial program, not $1 billion for each year of the two-year budget. And future funding will require additional legislative appropriations. Those are not Abbott’s dollars. They are your tax dollars.

NYT Today:
Republicans Are Worried About Gina Hinojosa. In Texas, I Saw Why. https://t.co/YyvdyIPjVU 
Republicans Are Worried About Gina Hinojosa. In Texas, I Saw Why.

Lynn Davenport, a lifelong conservative, metTrump backstage at a Texas rally in 2016. On Jan. 6, 2021, she was at his Stop the Steal rally in Washington, though she left before the Capitol was sacked. In 2024 she was a delegate to Texas’ Republican convention and a Republican precinct chair.

And in May she filmed an ad for Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running a surprisingly competitive race to become governor of Texas.
The two women have been friends for years, since Hinojosa, a state representative from Austin, helped lead opposition to a crusade by the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, to privatize Texas’ public school system. Abbott’s agenda was bitterly opposed by some conservative Texans, particularly rural ones in places where public schools are the center of the community. (Think “Friday Night Lights.”) Davenport was impressed by Hinojosa’s willingness to listen to her and by her mastery of education policy. Still, as a committed Republican, she didn’t think she’d ever vote for her.
The premise of Hinojosa’s surprisingly competitive campaign is that there’s a critical mass of voters like Davenport in Texas. The opportunity for Democrats, Hinojosa believes, lies not with moderate, affluent Republicans put off by Trump’s norm-smashing vulgarity but with disappointed MAGA populists. “The conventional political wisdom is that it is those country club Republicans who will swing over,” she told me before I traveled to Texas. “I think it’s always been MAGA.”

I was skeptical of this analysis then, and after seeing her campaign last week, I’m still not wholly convinced. Trump’s appeal has never been only or even primarily economic; he taps into fear and rage about a country growing less white, less Christian and less deferential to male authority. And Hinojosa seems, at least on paper, ill suited to appeal to Trump’s base. A Latina and a former labor lawyer, she comes from the heart of Texas’ Democratic establishment: Her father led the state Democratic Party from 2012 until 2025. Though she now calls herself a “populist” rather than a “progressive,” she’s one of the more liberal members of the Texas House.

Still, Hinojosa has a group of supporters like Davenport, people furious at Abbott over school privatization and data centers. Mary Lowe, an education activist and a self-described “fundamental Christian,” told me that Abbott is “a globalist. He’s a tyrant. He’s a great deceiver.” And though she has voted Republican in almost every primary and every general election since 1979, she’s voting for Hinojosa in November. “She’s a good human,” said Lowe. “She’s one of us.”
But Davenport has grown increasingly disgusted with Abbott, over both schools and the data centers he invited into Texas. The governor, she said, is a “globalist, which to me is scarier than a communist, a socialist or a Marxist, because what Abbott is imposing is technocracy. He’s giving the tech giants carte blanche in Texas.” So she decided not just to support Hinojosa’s bid for governor but to do it publicly. “Gina is someone that I can work with, whereas Abbott doesn’t care what I think,” she told me.

posts.text:
I think the point is that the polls can be so wildly off that not only do they produce final forecasts like this from the most "conservative"/cautious forecaster, Cook Political in 2020, but that also do a mediocre job of gauging general turnout.

Many people thought 2020 would be a repeat of 2016 and a build-up on top of 2018, but with higher turnout only favoring Democrats across the nation.  No one really expected 155 million total votes cast for president during Covid.

That's how you get ridiculous calls like Florida and California House seats as Likely D when they're eventually won by Republicans.  Or SC Senate as Tossup when Lindsey Graham was the incumbent candidate.  People just randomly expected Republicans to not show up for Trump.

Now it's a midterm.  But they showed up in 2022 when Trump wasn't really stumping for them.  Defied the October polls in red states (which people forget; even Greg Abbott was underestimated in Texas).  Showed up in 2024, of course.  And now Trump is holding rallies and campaigning to his base.

posts.text:
LAS ENCUESTAS FAVORECEN A LOS DEMÓCRATAS A 3 SEMANAS DE LAS ELECCIONES

Lectura rápida
Estados Unidos celebrará el 3 de noviembre elecciones de medio mandato que definirán si los republicanos conservan el control del Congreso. Los sondeos perfilan un escenario favorable para los demócratas en ambas cámaras. Trump intensifica su campaña con actos casi diarios en estados decisivos. La aprobación del presidente ronda el 38%.

Ventaja en la Cámara de Representantes
Se renovarán los 435 escaños y los demócratas necesitan una ganancia neta de tres para recuperar la mayoría. El promedio de encuestas de RealClearPolitics les otorga el 50,2% de intención de voto, frente al 41,9% de los republicanos. Cook Political Report estima que, con las tendencias actuales, podrían conquistar 18 distritos y superar los 230 asientos.

Siete estados clave para el Senado
Se renovarán 35 de los 100 escaños del Senado, donde los republicanos tienen una mayoría de 53 contra 47. Las contiendas están ajustadas en Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Míchigan, Ohio y Texas: los demócratas necesitan ganar cuatro bancas republicanas y conservar las propias para tomar el control. 

La disputa por las gobernaciones
Además, 36 estados elegirán gobernadores, con los demócratas Xavier Becerra y Kathy Hochul como favoritos en California y Nueva York. Los republicanos Greg Abbott y Byron Donalds lideran en Texas y Florida. Las contiendas siguen abiertas en Georgia, Nevada y Ohio, gobernados por republicanos, y en Wisconsin, en manos demócratas.
